title: Africa 4 of 8 · Central Africa
edition: Africa countries · Eight regional lessons · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Africa episode four of eight. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
Eight countries connect desert Chad with the Congo forests and Atlantic islands. São Tomé and Príncipe needs a labelled supplemental view because it is absent from GeoClick’s native map.

states.name: Chad
lines: Chad is landlocked below Libya, east of Niger and west of Sudan. Cameroon and the Central African Republic lie toward its south.
The lakes of Ounianga survive in a very dry Saharan landscape because groundwater feeds them. Some lakes are fresh and others salty, despite lying in the same desert region.
Picture surprising lakes in the desert above the Congo Basin. Chad is the tall inland link between Libya and the Central African Republic.
states.transition: Let's bring Chad and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Cameroon
lines: Cameroon lies southeast of Nigeria, with Chad toward its northeast and Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and the Republic of the Congo below. A southwestern coast reaches the Gulf of Guinea.
The Dja Faunal Reserve is almost encircled by the Dja River. Its forest supports many primates, with the river providing a remarkable natural boundary.
Remember a river loop around rainforest. Cameroon is the coastal hinge between West and Central Africa, below Nigeria’s eastern side.

states.name: Central African Republic
lines: The Central African Republic is landlocked below Chad and west of South Sudan. Cameroon lies west, with the two Congos toward its south.

The Sangha Trinational landscape joins protected forests in the Central African Republic, Cameroon and the Republic of the Congo. Forest clearings provide gathering places for elephants and other animals.
Picture elephants in a forest clearing at a three-country meeting. The Central African Republic sits inland above the Congo countries; its name describes its broad position.

states.name: Equatorial Guinea
lines: Equatorial Guinea includes a small mainland part below Cameroon, plus islands in the Gulf of Guinea. Bioko lies offshore; Gabon surrounds much of the mainland part.
This country’s geography is split between mainland and islands. Its name can mislead: the mainland is north of the equator, while the island of Annobón lies south of it.
Remember one country in separated pieces beside Cameroon and Gabon. Do not confuse Equatorial Guinea with Guinea or Guinea-Bissau on the West African coast.
states.transition: Let's bring Equatorial Guinea and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Gabon
lines: Gabon faces the Atlantic below Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon. The Republic of the Congo curves around its eastern and southern sides.
At Lopé-Okanda, rainforest meets older savannah patches. The landscape also preserves rock carvings and evidence of people moving through the Ogooué valley over long periods.
Picture forest beside savannah on the equatorial Atlantic coast. Gabon is west of the Republic of the Congo, with Equatorial Guinea tucked above it.
states.transition: Let's bring Gabon and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Republic of the Congo
lines: The Republic of the Congo lies east of Gabon and west of the much larger Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its short southwestern coastline reaches the Atlantic.
The Sangha forest landscape is shared with Cameroon and the Central African Republic. It connects protected habitats for forest elephants, gorillas and chimpanzees across national boundaries.
Remember Congo-Brazzaville as the smaller western Congo. Its neighbour across the great river is the Democratic Republic of the Congo; the similar names identify separate countries.
states.transition: Let's bring Republic of the Congo and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Democratic Republic of the Congo
lines: The Democratic Republic of the Congo occupies a vast central area east of the Republic of the Congo. It extends toward the Great Lakes in the east and has a very short Atlantic outlet.
Virunga National Park contains an extraordinary range of habitats, from volcanic landscapes to high mountains. Mountain gorillas live within this diverse eastern border region.
Picture a huge central basin reaching east to volcanoes and gorillas. This is Congo-Kinshasa, the larger Congo, not its smaller western neighbour.

states.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
lines: São Tomé and Príncipe is an Atlantic island country west of Gabon. Its two main islands lie in the Gulf of Guinea, separate from mainland Central Africa.
UNESCO’s Príncipe Biosphere Reserve recognises an island environment with distinctive forest and marine habitats. Isolation helps explain why island wildlife can differ from mainland wildlife.
Remember two islands off Gabon, not an extra mainland strip. Príncipe lies northeast of São Tomé; this labelled supplemental view keeps their real geographic positions.
states.factCredit: UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Programme

recap: Chad is above the Central African Republic. Cameroon reaches the Gulf of Guinea; Equatorial Guinea and Gabon follow the coast south. The smaller Republic of the Congo lies west of the much larger Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Recall desert lakes, a river-ringed forest, elephant clearings, mainland and island pieces, forest beside savannah and eastern volcanoes. São Tomé and Príncipe is offshore west of Gabon, not on the mainland.
